chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Hamzah said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: When a man marries a thayyib (previously married) woman who has been married to another husband, and she claims that he has not had intercourse with her since he entered into marriage with her, then the word in this matter is the man's, and it is upon him to swear by Allah that he has indeed had intercourse with her, because she is the claimant. He said: If he marries her while she is a virgin (bakr), and she claims that he has not reached her, then this case is known by women, so let a woman who is trustworthy among them look at her. If she says that she is a virgin, then it is upon the Imam to delay him for one year. If he has intercourse with her, then fine; otherwise, they are separated, and she is given half of the dowry, and there is no waiting period (iddah) upon her.

key_terms.الإمام: The Imam (or judge) who presides over the legal ruling
key_terms.الثّيّب: A woman who has been married before and is no longer a virgin
key_terms.العنة: Inability or refusal to consummate marriage
key_terms.العِدّة: Waiting period for a woman after divorce or death of husband

ai.seo_question: How does Shia jurisprudence determine proof of non-consummation of marriage for previously married versus virgin wives?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al-Ishtibār details the jurisprudential distinction in resolving 'unna' (consummation dispute) based on the wife’s marital history, reflecting the Imami school’s reliance on the husband’s oath for a previously married woman versus the verification of virginity for a first-time bride. It establishes a one-year grace period for the husband to consummate the marriage before a final divorce is enacted, ensuring fairness in the distribution of the mahr (dower). This ruling underscores the practical application of evidence standards in Shia family law, balancing the presumption of truth with the need for tangible proof in sensitive domestic matters.
